objective_text: Describe Azure regions, region pairs, and sovereign regions
option_a: A single building with its own power, cooling and networking
option_b: A geographical area containing at least one datacenter, or several nearby datacenters networked together with low latency
option_c: A billing boundary for Azure resources
option_d: A group of related policy definitions
why_correct: A region is a geographical area that contains at least one, and potentially several, nearby datacenters networked together with a low-latency network.
why_a_wrong: That describes a single datacenter, or the isolation of an availability zone, not a whole region.
why_c_wrong: A subscription is the billing unit, not a region.
why_d_wrong: A group of related policies is an Azure Policy initiative.
author: claude

objective_text: Describe Azure regions, region pairs, and sovereign regions
stem: Why are most Azure regions paired with another region in the same geography?
option_a: So that every Azure service automatically copies its data to the paired region
option_b: So the two regions can share a single datacenter
option_c: So that if a region is hit by a disaster, services can fail over to its pair
option_d: So data can move to a different geography at no cost
why_correct: If a region is affected by a disaster, services can fail over to the other region in its pair. Pairs are in the same geography, at least 300 miles apart.
why_a_wrong: Not all Azure services automatically replicate data, so some recovery must be configured by the customer.
why_b_wrong: Paired regions are at least 300 miles apart, so they do not share a datacenter.
why_d_wrong: Data stays within the same geography as its pair, with Brazil South as the exception.
author: claude

objective_text: Describe Azure regions, region pairs, and sovereign regions
stem: What is a sovereign region, such as US Gov Virginia or China East?
option_a: A region that has no datacenters
option_b: An isolated instance of Azure used for compliance or legal needs
option_d: A free region reserved for students
why_correct: Sovereign regions are isolated instances of Azure used for compliance or legal requirements, such as for US government agencies or China.
why_a_wrong: Sovereign regions do have datacenters and run as separate instances of Azure.
why_c_wrong: Availability zones sit inside a single region; sovereign regions are separate instances of Azure.
why_d_wrong: Sovereign regions exist for compliance and legal reasons, not as a student offer.
author: claude

stem: What is the minimum number of separate availability zones in a region that supports availability zones?
why_correct: A minimum of three separate availability zones are present in all availability zone-enabled regions.
why_a_wrong: The minimum is three, so one zone is not enough.
why_b_wrong: The minimum is three, so two zones would not meet it.
why_d_wrong: Three is the stated minimum, not five.
author: claude

option_a: A group of subscriptions under one management group
option_c: A physically separate datacenter within a region, with independent power, cooling and networking
option_d: A group of VMs that share a power or network failure point
why_correct: Availability zones are physically separate datacenters within an Azure region, each with independent power, cooling and networking, set up as an isolation boundary.
why_a_wrong: Management groups hold subscriptions; they are not availability zones.
why_b_wrong: A region pair is two regions, whereas zones are inside one region.
why_d_wrong: That describes a fault domain in an availability set, not an availability zone.
author: claude

stem: What do you find in an Azure datacenter?
option_a: A group of resources that share a lifecycle
option_c: A rule that audits resource settings
option_d: Servers in racks, with dedicated power, cooling and networking
why_correct: Datacenters are facilities with servers in racks and dedicated power, cooling and networking. They are grouped into regions and availability zones.
why_a_wrong: That describes a resource group, not a datacenter.
why_b_wrong: Subscriptions are billing units and are not part of the physical facility.
why_c_wrong: That describes Azure Policy, not a datacenter.
author: claude

objective_text: Describe Azure resources and resource groups
stem: What happens when you delete a resource group?
option_a: Everything in the group is deleted
option_b: Only the group's name is removed and its resources move to the subscription
option_c: Its resources move to another resource group automatically
option_d: Nothing happens, because resource groups cannot be deleted
why_correct: Deleting a resource group deletes everything in it.
why_b_wrong: The resources are not kept; they are deleted with the group.
why_c_wrong: Resources are not moved automatically when a group is deleted.
why_d_wrong: Resource groups can be deleted, and doing so deletes their contents.
author: claude

objective_text: Describe Azure resources and resource groups
stem: Which statement about Azure resource groups is correct?
option_a: A resource can belong to two resource groups at once
option_b: Resource groups can be nested inside each other
option_c: Every resource must belong to exactly one resource group
option_d: A resource group can be renamed at any time after creation
why_correct: Every resource must belong to exactly one resource group, though some resources can be moved between groups.
why_a_wrong: A resource is associated with only one group at a time.
why_d_wrong: Resource groups cannot be renamed after creation.
author: claude

stem: How does Azure describe a subscription?
option_b: A unit of management, billing and scale
option_c: A geographical area with nearby datacenters
option_d: A name and value label on a resource
why_correct: A subscription is a unit of management, billing and scale. Azure generates separate billing reports and invoices for each subscription.
why_a_wrong: A separate datacenter is an availability zone or datacenter, not a subscription.
why_c_wrong: A geographical area is a region.
why_d_wrong: A name and value label is a tag.
author: claude

stem: How many levels deep can management groups be nested, not counting the root level or the subscription level?
why_correct: Management groups can be nested up to six levels deep, not counting the root level or the subscription level.
why_a_wrong: Six is the limit, so two is below it.
why_b_wrong: Six is the limit, so four is below it.
why_d_wrong: Six is the limit, so ten is above it.
author: claude

objective_text: Describe the hierarchy of resource groups, subscriptions, and management groups
stem: Which order shows the Azure hierarchy from top to bottom?
option_a: Resource groups, subscriptions, management groups, resources
option_b: Subscriptions, management groups, resources, resource groups
option_c: Management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, resources
option_d: Resources, resource groups, subscriptions, management groups
why_correct: Management groups sit above subscriptions, subscriptions contain resource groups, and resource groups contain resources. Policies and access inherit downward.
why_a_wrong: Management groups sit above subscriptions, not below resource groups.
why_b_wrong: Subscriptions contain resource groups, which contain resources, so this order is mixed up.
why_d_wrong: That order runs from bottom to top, not top to bottom.
author: claude
